SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

president noun

the head of state of a republic

also the president, presidential, vice-president, vice president, president-elect, head of state

modern

Traupman 364: president
M-O s.v. president (of nation)

praeses, praesidis m./f.

noun, third declension, masculine or feminine

the president of a country

Classically one who presides over or guards something: the senate was the state’s custōs, praeses, prōpugnātor (Cic. Sest. 137, Lewis & Short), and under the emperors a praeses governed a province. Morgan–Owens takes it for the president of a nation from twentieth-century Latin (Perugini, Egger), with praeses dēsignātus, the president-elect, and praesidis vicārius, the vice-president. The Roman republic had no president: its highest office was held by two consuls (see office, a public office).

Examples

  • Omnīnō quī reī pūblicae praefutūrī sunt duo Platōnis praecepta teneant

    Those who are to be at the head of the state should keep two rules of Plato’sCic. Off. 1.85

Other words

  • praesidēns, praesidentis m. — the president of a country

    noun, third declension · also used · modern · Traupman 180; vice praesidēns, vice president, Traupman 181

    Traupman’s other word: the present participle of praesideō, “preside”, used as a noun.

  • prīnceps reī pūblicae — the head of state

    phrase · also used · modern · M-O s.v. president: head of state

    Classically prīnceps cīvitātis was a leading statesman, and prīnceps became the emperor’s title (see leader).

  • quī reī pūblicae praeest — the one at the head of the state

    phrase: praesum with the dative · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.85: quī reī pūblicae praefutūrī sunt

    A classical way round the title: praeesse, be at the head of, with the dative.

See also president, leader, government, state, office.

SourcesLewis & Short: praeses · Lewis & Short: praesideo · Lewis & Short: princeps · Lewis & Short: praesum
